opus-5.5.text:
I think the relationship is actually quite subtle, and in some ways counterintuitive.

On the surface, you'd expect the winners of the previous era to have every advantage: more capital, more talent, more data, more distribution. And those things do matter. But what I've observed is that success in one paradigm often creates a kind of gravity that pulls you back toward that paradigm. Your organization is built around it. Your incentives, your KPIs, your promotion system, even the way people talk in meetings: all of it is optimized for what worked last time.

Take the previous wave of AI, the era of recommendation systems, computer vision, task-specific models. The companies that did extremely well there had very strong engineering cultures for building many specialized models and deploying them at scale. That was the right answer for that time. But large language models required something quite different: a willingness to bet enormous resources on a single, very general model, and to tolerate a long period where it wasn't obvious the bet would pay off. If your organization is used to clear, quarter-by-quarter returns from many smaller projects, making that kind of concentrated bet is psychologically and structurally very hard.

So I'd say previous success is neither a guarantee nor a curse. It's an asset only if you can stay honest about which parts of it are truly transferable. Compute infrastructure, engineering excellence, talent density: those transfer. But beliefs about how research should be organized, what counts as progress, who gets to make decisions, those often don't.

What I think matters most for the next era is the ability to keep a very pure focus on the core technical question, and to let young, curious people work on it with a lot of freedom. Many of the most important ideas in recent years didn't come from the most senior people. They came from people who didn't yet know what was "supposed" to be impossible. A leader from the previous era who can create that kind of environment can absolutely lead again. One who just tries to replicate the old playbook at a bigger scale probably won't.

And honestly, this applies to all of us now as well. Whatever is working today in large models will, at some point, become the old paradigm. The real test is whether we can notice that moment when it comes.

r001.rationale: The response says previous success is “neither a guarantee nor a curse” and that leaders who repeat the old playbook probably will not lead again.

r002.rationale: The response discusses transferable advantages and challenges for established companies, but does not say new-era participants are on roughly the same starting line.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that relationship is actually much weaker than people assume, and in some ways it's inverted. Being very successful in the last era can become a burden in the next one, because the things that made you win — your data pipelines, your product habits, your organizational structure, your sense of what "good" looks like — were all optimized for a paradigm that is now shifting underneath you.

Look at how this has played out historically. The companies that dominated PCs weren't the ones that dominated mobile. The leaders in search weren't automatically the leaders in recommendation. Each wave rewards a slightly different combination of skills, and the previous winners tend to be slow precisely because they have something to protect. When you have a very profitable existing business, every new direction gets evaluated against it, and a new paradigm usually looks small and unprofitable at the beginning. That's exactly when you need to commit to it, and exactly when a successful incumbent finds it hardest to do so.

I'd also say that the skills themselves have changed. The previous era was largely about applying models to vertical problems — you'd train something for a specific task, you'd tune it, you'd deploy it. The current era is about building general capability, and that's a fundamentally different kind of work. It's closer to basic research than product engineering. It requires patience with long-horizon bets, tolerance for a lot of failed experiments, and a very dense concentration of talent who genuinely understand the frontier. Those are not things you can simply buy with the resources you accumulated last time.

That said, I don't want to be too absolute about it. Capital, compute, and distribution still matter a lot, and the previous winners do have those. What I'd argue is that they're necessary but not sufficient. What becomes decisive is whether an organization can honestly reset its own assumptions — treat itself as a beginner again, let younger people with fresher instincts drive the technical direction, and accept that some of its hard-won experience is now wrong.

So my view is: previous success buys you a ticket to the game, not a lead in it. The lead goes to whoever is most willing to unlearn.

r001.rationale: The response says prior success has a much weaker-than-assumed relationship with future leadership and that it buys a ticket, not a lead.

r002.rationale: It says prior winners retain advantages such as capital, compute, and distribution; it does not state that participants are roughly on the same starting line.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think success in the previous AI era automatically translates into leadership in the next one. It gives you advantages—experience, talent, resources—but it can also make you more attached to the approaches that worked before.

When the underlying technology changes, some of those advantages carry over, and others become less relevant. The challenge is recognizing which is which. Can you question your own assumptions? Can you invest in a direction that might undermine your existing strengths?

So I’d look less at who won the last round and more at who keeps learning and adapting. Past success is a foundation, but it isn’t a guarantee.

r001.rationale: It says prior-era success does not automatically translate into leadership in the next era.

r002.rationale: It discusses advantages and adaptation but does not state that participants in the new era are on roughly the same starting line.

I don’t think success in one era automatically translates into leadership in the next. It gives you advantages—talent, resources, experience—but it can also make you more attached to the assumptions that worked before.

When the technology changes, the important question is whether you can recognize what has changed and rethink your approach. Sometimes that means letting go of something you’re very good at. So I’d see past success as a foundation, rather than a guarantee. Leadership in the next era still has to be earned through learning, judgment, and execution.
